newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. council wants Angola unity government set up.
newsitem.headline: U.N. council wants Angola unity government set up.

text.p: The Security Council expressed deep concern on Thursday at the delay in forming a government of national unity and reconciliation in Angola, blaming former UNITA rebels for failing to meet an agreed timetable.

A statement read at a brief council meeting called on UNITA and the Angolan government to strictly implement an agreement setting out a new timetable and to form the unity government "without any linkages and without further delay."
Inauguration of the new government, called for under a 1994 peace accord ending 20 years of civil war, had been set for Jan. 25.
It was postponed after negotiations failed to find an acceptable role for UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi, who still controls much of Angola, including diamond-rich areas.

The Security Council noted that, at a Jan. 23 meeting at which the delay was announced, UNITA agreed to ensure all of its National Assembly deputies and members of the future unity government would be in Luanda, the capital, on Feb. 12. The government undertook to set a new date for the inauguration of the new administration immediately after the arrival of the UNITA deputies.

"Failure to implement this agreement could jeopardise the peace process and lead the Security Council to consider appropriate measures ... against those responsible for the delays," the council statement said.

It also noted with concern the slow pace at which remaining military aspects of the 1994 peace accord were being implemented, particularly a delay in demobilizing and integrating UNITA soldiers into the Angolan Armed Forces.
A 7,000-strong U.N. force called UNAVEM III (U.N. Angola Verification Mission III), whose mandate expires at the end of February, has been helping implement the peace process.

The council emphasised that the ultimate responsibility for restoring peace rested with the Angolans themselves. It reminded both sides that the international community could provide assistance only if progress were achieved in the peace process and that it would consider a U.N. presence in Angola after the expiration of UNAVEM III's mandate "in this context."
